_note: Core methodological vocabulary (Inventory: Core Vocabulary + recurring concepts). Used for term<->definition multiple choice.

terms.def: The entity each row of the data describes (e.g., a résumé, a voter, a restaurant, a state).
An observation is one unit's record (a row); a variable is one measured characteristic across units (a column).
The number of observations in the data used for an analysis.
The causal variable of interest, whose effect on an outcome we want to learn; it need not be medical.
The variable a study tries to explain or predict; its values are compared across treatment conditions.
The units that receive the treatment (T = 1).
The units that do not receive the treatment (T = 0), whose outcomes stand in for the treated units' counterfactuals.
A characteristic measured or determined before treatment is assigned, so the treatment cannot affect it.
What would have happened to a unit if a key condition, such as its treatment status, had been different.
The outcomes Y(1) and Y(0) a unit would have under treatment and under control; only one is ever observed.
Data from a design in which the researcher manipulates the treatment variable to study its effect on the outcome.
A study in which the researcher does not intervene but observes naturally occurring treatment and collects data.
An observational setting in which treatment is assigned as if at random by nature or circumstance, not by the researcher.
Multiple measurements taken over time on the same units.
Comparing treated and control units measured at the same point in time after treatment.
Confounding bias that arises because units self-select into the treatment.
Comparing pretreatment covariates across treatment groups to see whether the groups are similar, as randomization should make them.
A variable taking the value 1 if a condition holds and 0 otherwise; its mean is the proportion of 1s.
A categorical variable that takes a finite number of distinct values, called levels.
A cross-tabulation of the number of observations in each combination of categories of two or more variables.
The average outcome in the treatment group minus the average outcome in the control group.
The sample average treatment effect for the treated: the average causal effect among the treated units only.
Without treatment, the treated group's outcome would have followed the same time trend as the control group's.
The full set of units a researcher wants to learn about by studying a sample.
The complete list of potential respondents from which a sample is drawn.
Interviewing fixed quotas of respondents with certain characteristics so the sample matches the population on those observed traits.
Sampling larger units first (e.g., districts), then randomly selecting smaller units (villages, households) within the selected ones.
Respondents give the answer seen as socially acceptable rather than their truthful answer.
Respondents report only how many list items they support; the treatment list adds a sensitive item, and the difference in mean counts estimates support for it.
In a list experiment, answering the minimum (0) or maximum count reveals a respondent's true answer to the sensitive item.
Respondents privately randomize (e.g., roll a die) to decide whether to answer honestly, protecting individual answers while allowing aggregate estimates.
Dropping every observation that has a missing value on at least one variable.
An unobservable characteristic, such as ideology or ability, that must be measured through a model of observed behavior.
A legislator's most preferred position in a spatial model of ideology; they vote for whichever option (proposal or status quo) is closer to it.
A class of measurement models from educational testing that estimate examinees' abilities and questions' difficulties from their answers.
The ideological centers of the two parties moving apart over time.
A curve plotting the cumulative share of income against the cumulative share of people sorted from lowest to highest income.
Methods, such as clustering, that discover hidden structure in data without an outcome variable.
The center of a cluster, equal to the within-cluster mean of each variable.
The observed outcome minus its fitted value from a model.
The value of the outcome a model predicts for a given value of the predictor.
The sum of squared deviations of the outcome from its mean: the outcome's total variation.
Tailoring a model so closely to one sample that it predicts poorly in other samples.
An observation whose value is extremely different from the rest of the data, such as one with a very large residual.
The factor level omitted from a regression with an intercept; other levels' coefficients are measured relative to it.
The number of observations free to vary: the number of observations minus the number of estimated parameters (\(n - p - 1\)).
Treatment effects that differ in size or direction across units or subgroups.
Holding all other predictors constant when interpreting one coefficient.
Estimating an effect that is known to be zero in theory, such as an effect on a past outcome, to check a design's validity.
A table cross-classifying predicted and actual outcomes into true positives, false positives, false negatives, and true negatives.
A candidate's votes divided by the votes cast for the two major-party candidates only.
